title: Music in a Dark Room
chapters: The memory of one bad school show still lived with Mina, and she did not want that again. Her father held down two jobs and still was at her Friday practice. Mina held to one rule: the music had to be honest. The old guitar brought back a summer memory of her grandma. Mina, Joon, and Sara headed off for the music room after class. Ms Park asked them to black out their home addresses on the concert form. Mina did not want anyone in the room to sit around with work to do. Their group had one month to plan a show for the families.

Sara had to sit for the baby of her cousin that evening, but she agreed to come. Mina sat up late and wrote a new opening. A month of work had to end in a successful concert. At the classroom door, Joon stood aside for a woman with a large drum. Ms Park asked the group to stand back from their personal ideas and think about the full show. They would not stand by as the music club lost the room. Mina stood up and described her goal. Everyone listened because her words were easy and true. The room became quiet, and the team began to feel like a real band.

The children met with Ms Park at a round table. They set forth for the town music shop with a list and a little money. Joon watched for the number seven bus. At the shop, Mina and Joon faced off about a guitar and a drum. Sara added three bells to the order, and the price became large. Mina began to grow in skill as she explained her idea. The shop man opened out a paper map of the music room. He showed them a piano, a radio, and a computer on the map. The group had to choose the thing their show really needed.

Joon wanted to walk around in tiger clothes during the opening. Mina started to walk away because the idea felt funny. Ms Park told Joon not to walk over Mina or make her do his work. She walked the team through the music from the start to the end. A healthy meal could build up the tired children. Ms Park asked them to stay away from a broken light on the wall. Sara ate bread and fruit, and the meal stayed down. Joon said sorry to Mina and put the tiger cap back in the box. Mina said that was fine, and their conversation became warm.

After a healthy summer, Joon had lost fat, and it stayed off. The group planned on practice for one hour after school. Sara cut up apples, bananas, and cheese for the team. Bad music could drive away the families, so everyone listened carefully. A late order could drive up the ticket price. A little bell began to break away from the old line. Sara's face broke out after she touched some old cream. Ms Park washed her face and gave her clean water. Sara felt better, and she went to the table with a smile.

Mina picked over the clothes for the concert. Her mobile rang, and her mom asked her to phone back after practice. Sara had to cover for Joon when he went to the doctor. Mina had to step back to see the full plan. Loud music made the baby draw away from the music room door. Ms Park drew a blue cloth back from the old piano. At six, the bus drew into the school yard. The children put the guitar, bells, paper, and food in bags. They were tired, but their opening practice had given the band a clear character.

On Friday evening, Mina wrote ten questions for a family survey. She wanted to know the music type the town liked. Joon made a video, Sara designed a card, and Ms Park checked the spelling. The group chose a personal story for the opening and their favorite music for the end. Mina wrote the date, time, site, and ticket number on the form. The class would share the news through a magazine, a television message, and a school article. Their goal was not to be famous or rich. They wanted a careful place for a kid to learn a skill, meet a classmate, and make music.

Mina laughed. "Remember me when you write the book," she said. She was just happy to have a role. The club was not only about a win. Music was very important, and homework was too. Mina never forgot this point. The turn was Leo's. He began speaking. In that case, he would always be ready. Members must practice, but they could enjoy it. The book had four sections about music history, and one period covered the guitar. Music was Leo's favorite subject. The children often spent almost an hour with the book. Later, someone brought a new book. Once the group began reading, anything could happen in their ideas. Maybe everything would be ready soon. A school officer came quickly with a fine message. A poor family usually saved money, but the club could save a seat for their child.

On Saturday morning, the school bus began to close on a slow taxi. Snow had banked up at the side of the road. Mina threw back her blanket, wore jeans and a coat, ran fast, and opened the door. Sara topped up three cups with water for the show. Bread, eggs, and fruit filled Joon up at breakfast. On the walk to school, Joon began to drop back. He dropped behind Mina and Sara because his drum was heavy. He talked about dropping out of the show, but Mina asked him to wait. They shared the drum and were at the school as one.

A power problem pushed the concert back from morning to afternoon. Parents began to push for a clear answer. Ms Park pushed forward with a new plan, even without the computer. A rude guy tried to push in at the office line. His large bag pushed a chair over, and he said sorry. Mina signed out a guitar, a drum, and a radio. Sara checked on the young children in the dark classroom. Joon learned to laugh at being afraid of the dark. The team finished off the food and began a meeting. Ms Park shook up the music club and gave the children new jobs.

Mina's cousin planned to fly into town for the show. Her uncle went to fish for dinner at the lake. Sara wished for sunshine and warm weather. A jet touched down at the airport during the rain. Joon wanted to sleep the afternoon away, but Mina kept him awake. Ms Park chose to sleep on the question of moving the concert. Children fanned out through the hall to find candles and a radio. The parents drank to the future of the band with tea. Joon drank up his juice and stood. The class banded together around the large windows.

Joon's shirt began to ride up as he lifted the drum. The dark room warmed up with time in the afternoon sun. Wind blew a small tree down in the yard. It also blew Sara's cap off. Everyone had to bone up on a careful rule. Rain fell, and small leaves rained down on the roof. Mina dried her guitar off with a soft towel. Gray began to nose around the closed office. Joon and Sara kicked around the room without a plan. Their three ideas did not match up at the start.

The school planned to grass over a dirty part of the yard. Rain washed a blue line off the board. Mina breathed out and began to feel calm. Sara toyed with a gold ring when she was nervous. The children dug grass in around a small plant. Mr Han dug over the wet ground and dug up an old black box. The new concert plan was shaping up. Mina struck off to the library with the box. A shy boy, Leo, wanted to fit in, so Sara gave him two bells. Gray hit back when Ms Park asked about the office door.

An old wall in the basement had started to fall in. Ticket sales had fallen off after the power news. Still, families began to roll in from around town. Mr Han stamped out a small fire from a candle. The students tidied up the hall and spread out blankets at the windows. Ms Park followed up on the power news by telephone. The young children fell back from the dark basement. The job of keeping the children well fell on Ms Park. She asked everyone to lie down on the blankets and listen. They could count on her, and the room became calm.

The children used easy things to test the new music. Cups held water, a box became a drum, and two spoons made a clear beat. A bottle, a dish, and a bell made new notes. Mina wrote the test results in a file. Sara took a photo of the room and posted it to the school site. Their video was watched ten times, then twenty, then fifty. A family from the library gave a message of help. The power was still gone, but the music had already started.

At the weekend, Ms Park opened a new section of the rule book. She gave a nice example and asked a child, "Imagine yourself at peace after a show." A bar on an old machine held one small item. Joon's shoulder and neck began to hurt after he lifted it. Sara explained that the brain, eye, and ear help a child balance. Anybody could jump in the game, but a sick child had to sit. A student with a high grade worked with a young child as a pair. They wrote a name and birth date in the bottom row of a form. The code used a thin line for a small problem and a thick line for a large one. Gray tried to judge the children, but Ms Park asked him to solve the strange topic with them. At lunch, half the group ate meat and half ate rice. Leo had to repeat the rule because the bell was not in his sight. A surprise came when an interested boy found a toy ship at the hill. One wheel was gone. The children looked everywhere and found it by a box with living things.

Sara added water to the cups until the notes evened out. Anyone could lose out because the computer was dark, and the group did not want that. Joon sent up Gray's important way of talking, and even Gray had to laugh. His trousers were not tight and fell down, and the group laughed again. A tall box fell over, but the glass did not break. A bus passed by the window as their small practice passed off well. A truck pulled up with boards, cloth, and tools. Mr Han tried to explain away the old wall as a small matter. Mina hit on a careful idea: use the bright library room. The students cleared away the broken boxes.

Mina struck out a dangerous line in the plan. Sara tied up the jobs at the end for the move. The library wanted to cash in on the new concert news, but it gave the room for free. Joon mixed up two bags and gave Ms Park the wrong file. The shop knocked down the price of the bells. A child was locked in the music room for one minute, and Mr Han opened the door. Ms Park rounded up the students and checked the names. The meaning of the power problem began to sink in. Families could tune in to the radio, but they could not see the children. Mina boiled the plan down to one sentence: make honest music in a bright room.

Joon was afraid that he would screw up the opening. On the way to the library, the bus pulled over for a sick passenger. Gray hit out at the slow trip, but Mina asked him to be calm. Ms Park told Gray to clear off if he could not be polite. Gray chose to stay and sounded off about the late concert. The library fitted out a large room with tables and seats. Mr Han fixed up the old piano. The children knocked about ideas for the opening. Ms Park knocked back a plan that used fire. At five, everyone knocked off and went home.

Gray tried to shout Mina down during the end talk. The library door locked him out when he stepped into the yard. He asked Sara to string along with his story, but she gave the true words. Gray gave Mina an angry answer, and she bit back with angry words. Joon tuned out the fight and kept practicing. In the kitchen, soup boiled over, so Sara closed the kitchen fire. Her mom boiled up fresh water and made tea. Sara sewed up a hole in Joon's cloth bag. Joon did not want to part with his old drum, even when the drum cloth broke. The shop agreed to force the price down.

Ms Park sent for a piano man. She sent Mina off with the finished room form and sent Joon out to buy a chain. When Leo wore the tiger cap, the children fell about laughing. Ms Park put the class into groups that fell into music, food, and design. Gray and Joon fell out about the opening. The hard job fell to Mina. She asked Gray and Joon to report back after a quiet conversation. In the yard, a taxi pulled away and a truck pulled in. The bus man pulled back from a dangerous trip. The piano man pulled into the library yard in the evening.

The broken piano returned to a clear note after the fix. Mina's cousin landed in town on the evening jet. Tools and bags were lying around the library floor. A tired Joon lay back on a couch. The old radio began to act up, and Mina feared for the Saturday show. Joon struck at a baseball in the yard to clear his mind. From the open window, Sara struck up quiet music on the piano. Mina rolled up the arms of her shirt and began her job. The boxes fit into the truck, and the band crossed over from power music to music made by hand. Mr Han waved the truck through the school door. The dark room reminded Mina of the bad show she still remembered.

At home, Mina made a list of roles for the concert. Sara would play piano, Joon would play the box drum, Leo would ring the bells, and Mina would play guitar. Gray would introduce the group and read the family survey. Ms Park would welcome the visitors and explain the power problem. A mom would give soup, salad, rice, chicken, and sweet corn. A dad would carry chairs, tables, and blankets. The easy order helped everyone understand the full plan. Mina slept with the guitar by her bed and had a dream of a bright room.

The group went shopping at the supermarket for concert things. Mina said hello to Mr Smith and asked, "Sir, is this tube of gold paint for you?" Mr Smith said it was hers now because the club had given money for it. The bread section had a lovely smell. Joon bought meat, rice, and a chocolate bar, and Sara bought soap for the shower and bath. A young man and his girlfriend came. A young woman and her boyfriend came. The handsome young man gave his dear girlfriend a short kiss. Gray made an excuse when a rat jumped from the garbage by the toilet. Mina had a headache, but the surprise made her laugh. The box size was on a blank page. The sum was fifteen dollars, and the shop gave the club a super bag for everyday use.

After shopping, the group took the subway to a cinema. A foreigner from Mina's hometown held an umbrella and a pretty flag. He said hi, and Mina answered hello. His hobby was to surf, and his own video was about a princess at sea. The cinema ticket was eleven dollars for a child, thirteen for a student, seventeen for a parent, eighteen for a foreigner, and nineteen for Mr Smith. A school group had seventy tickets in the same row. Leo played spy with a ruler and hid at a large vase. Ms Park asked him to hurry because the movie was due to start. Leo said pardon, put the ruler back, and felt merry. At the door he said bye and asked the band plan for Sunday.

On Friday night, Ms Park would not shut a nervous child away from the group. She shut out the loud street music by closing the windows. The guitar belonged to Mina's grandfather, and the guitar music felt personal. Students emptied out the bags and marked ticket prices down. The road to the library branched off at a temple. Mina fixed her eyes on the concert card. Sara poured out her worry: would anyone come? Gray tore the old picture apart, and Mina tore up a false card. A cup tipped over and wet the end plan. The team divided up the jobs and started again.

They knocked around a new name for the show. Leo shouted out Music in a Dark Room, and everyone liked it. Ms Park locked the ticket money away in a bank box. Joon dusted off his jacket by the piano. A parent weighed in with an idea for a family conversation after the show. Gray disagreed with the plan because it was not honest. He hung about at the door and did nothing. Mina tossed up a round piece of money to choose between the two plans. Mr Han connected up the radio and the computer. The library laid on tea, cream, and chocolate for the visitors.

The young children settled down on a soft carpet. Gray messed up the opening talk but did not leave. He liked to hang out with the band, even when he acted strong. Joon had been laid up with a fever in January, and he remembered missing music. Gray told Leo not to mess with Mina or make her angry. Leo stuck at his bell practice. Mr Han switched on the wall light. Families began to rise up from their seats when the music started. Ms Park laid down one rule: listen to the children. Gray asked everyone to hang on as he found the right card.

The group stuck to the easy opening. The guitar, piano, drum, cups, and bells hung together. Gray asked if his opening talk would measure up. The hot sun beat down on the library roof. The children stuck together when one cup broke. Mina stuck with the plan made by hand. The library owner wanted computer music, but she caved in after hearing the cups. Sara pinned down the correct water level for the notes. A cloth filtered the dirty part out of the water. After the long practice, Joon crashed out on the couch.

Ms Park nailed down the Saturday order with the library owner. Mina pinned up photos from the dark school room. Sara ticked off the finished jobs. The old radio ticked over in the corner. Joon reduced a cookie to small pieces on his plate. Mina laid the old plan aside. Some children wanted to hang around, but Ms Park asked the children to go home. The band had beaten out a music club for the library room. Their show related to real family life, and the waitress attended to the food tables. Even after a new power call, the group pressed ahead.

Leo stuck up his hand and asked to join the full band. He had settled into the group and was not shy now. Joon lifted up the drum and gave Leo a seat. Sara pulled a pink cloth, and it stretched to sixty feet. She wrapped the cloth round a bright bottle. Gray tried to drag Joon into a new fight. Their talk dragged on until Ms Park stopped it. She said that a rude member could be booted out. Joon switched the radio over to the news. The weather news said that a strong wind and heavy rain would be in town on Saturday.

The band checked the weather, the bus time, and the library phone number. Mina made sure that the center door, bathroom, and red light were easy to find. Ms Park wrote a short careful paragraph for the families. Mr Han checked the roof, windows, and floor. Sara put towels, water, and a doctor box in a box at a table. Gray practiced his opening talk without a funny line. Leo played the bells at the right moment. The bad weather was coming, but the group was ready for it.

While the band waited, Gray got mail from a national radio club. The state music system wanted to play their video in a million homes. Most children thought a million was a lot, though Mina cared about the town families most. The power issue had traveled far from the school. Among the club members, Gray was the most surprised. He had never imagined himself on national radio. The law allowed a child video within the school system, but the music had to stay low. Gray said that good luck had changed his old self. He asked the group to pray for peace during the concert. The office was closed, but Gray himself wrote the answer and put it in the mail.

On Saturday, the band polished off a fast pizza as the visitors arrived. Sara wiped out the wet cups with a towel. Mina's calm focus began to rub off on Gray. Parents pitched in with chairs and food. Joon shrugged off a bad opening beat. Mr Han hooked up the radio to a mobile phone. Sara weeded out two false notes. A pet cat curled up at the piano. Gray snapped up the job of welcoming a late family. He did not spin out the opening talk this time.

In the kitchen, a mom put sugar with butter, then rubbed the butter in. Mina rubbed out a wrong time on the board. Leo's tiger cap made the little kids crack up. Parents stacked up clean plates and cups. Sara pegged out wet cloths in the yard. The library wanted to profit from the ticket sale, but it gave the money to the club. Mr Han chipped away old paint from the window. Joon swung at a baseball during the lunch break. When the band started, Mina was swept away by the music. After the meal, Gray swept up the floor.

The heavy rain arrived during the new music. Wind shook the windows, and rain fell on the roof. The power stopped, but the band did not stop. Mina played guitar, Joon held the beat, Sara played piano, and Leo rang the bells. Gray held a candle at the back wall. The visitors became quiet, and then they gave the band a loud call. A baby smiled, an old man cried, and a young girl made a video. The room was dark, but the music was warm and clear. Mina knew that the show had become something special.

After the end note, everyone stayed in the library until the rain became light. Ms Park gave soup and tea. Families talked about school, work, healthy care, travel, sport, culture, and technology. A cop thanked them for the careful plan. A coach asked the band to play in a football game. A magazine woman wanted an interview, and a television site wanted the video. Gray answered the questions without acting like a star. He thanked Mina, Joon, Sara, Leo, Ms Park, Mr Han, and the families. The power problem had changed him.

The ticket count was ninety, and the group had sold eighty cups of tea. Ten young children, twelve parents, fourteen students, and sixteen old guests had written names on the club list. The food table had five cakes, six pizzas, seven salads, eight rice dishes, nine bowls of soup, and twenty bottles of water. A family gave thirty dollars, a factory gave forty, and the library gave fifty. The group did not care about becoming rich. The numbers meant that the school music room could open again and that the club could buy careful tools.

The children left the library late in the evening. A taxi took Sara and Leo home. Joon rode his bike with his dad, and Mina walked with her mum. The wet road was bright with the street light. Mina carried the guitar in one hand and the concert card in her bag. She was tired, but her heart felt full. At home, she put the card on a shelf by a family album. She knew she would remember the dark room through her life.

On Monday, the class reviewed the concert. Ms Park asked everyone to describe a best moment and a difficult moment. Mina chose the quiet moment after the power stopped. Joon chose the call from the football coach. Sara chose the young boy with the bells. Leo chose the laughing from his tiger cap. Gray chose his honest thanks at the end. The children learned that a successful show was not a perfect result. It was a group that stayed as one when something went wrong.

The class voted for a new music club. Mina became the leader, Joon became the drum coach, Sara had the piano job, Leo taught bells, and Gray had the news job. Ms Park wrote the club rules on the board. Members had to be careful, kind, correct, and on time. Not one member could fight, hide tools, or be bad to a new kid. Anyone could ask a question, share an idea, or review an answer. The rules were strict but fair. Everyone wrote a name on the page and got a small green card.

The club made a calendar for the year. January would bring a piano afternoon, February a love music evening, March a spring concert, and April a rain show. May would have a family picnic, June a guitar contest, July a beach festival, and August a summer video. September would bring a school concert, October a ghost drama, November an autumn meal, and December a winter party. Monday was for planning, Tuesday for guitar, Wednesday for piano, Thursday for drums, Friday for the full band, Saturday for a town show, and Sunday for sleep. The long calendar made the future feel real.

Children chose music from around the world. Prince music from a palace, fairy music from a forest, an opera from a city, and a poem from a village were on the list. A Korean drum, a Spanish guitar, British pop music, and a foreign dance gave the club many music types. One child brought an album, a boy brought a mobile video, and a classmate brought a dictionary for foreign words. Ms Park taught grammar through music sentences. The children learned to spell names, write paragraphs, and introduce characters. Music had become a new language course.

The club also planned food and clothes for the events. There would be pizza, hamburgers, chicken, beef, turkey, rice, beans, corn, salad, soup, chocolate, candy, grapes, and tea. Children could wear trousers, pants, jeans, a skirt, a dress, an apron, a cap, or glasses. A doll, a toy bear, a frog, a tiger, a lion, a monkey, a pig, a snake, a mouse, a butterfly, and a bee would be in the room. A rose, a lily, a leaf, and sunshine would be on the spring cards. The design group had many ideas, but it agreed not to make the room ugly or crowded.

At the opening club meeting, a girl played volleyball with a balloon, and a boy used a baseball bat like a drum. A soccer fan wore a red cap, and a tennis coach brought a bat. A basketball girl showed the way a strong beat could match a fast step. A fishing guest played a quiet note on a bottle, and a farmer used a bucket as a drum. A waitress gave juice, and a shop owner gave the club a low price. Grandma sat on a sofa, Grandpa sat in a couch, and a grandparent held a tired baby. The club welcomed everybody, from a shy kid to a smart parent.

Mina saw the dark computer and smiled. The power problem had seemed terrible, but it had provided a reason to change. The club now included kids from many levels, families from around town, and members from a foreign country. It allowed personal stories, social goals, careful research, and honest pleasure. Members would use technology when it helped, but they understood that music did not depend on power. The fact was easy: a bottle, a box, a spoon, a call, and a group of classmates could fill a room with life. It was the best show Mina had ever known. The children were doing the thing they loved. Mina touched the old guitar, and the new club began.
